title: The First Public AI Lab Has to Prove a Software Margin
subtitle: Anthropic raised $119 billion to sell intelligence by the token, but its prospectus reveals a business tethered to the cloud.
summary: Anthropic's record public debut gives the market its first audited look at the unit economics of frontier AI. With revenue growth decelerating and nearly a trillion dollars of compute commitments on the books, the company has to prove it can earn software-grade margins rather than wholesale cloud capacity.

bodyHtml:
Monday was supposed to be a victory lap for the artificial intelligence complex. Nvidia rallied more than 30% after reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, and the Nasdaq staged its sharpest single-day rebound in over eighteen months.

Anthropic, which had just completed the largest public listing on record, quietly lost ground. While the sector celebrated, the market's newest pure-play AI bellwether slipped into the red, uncomfortably close to its $83 offer price.

The disconnect comes down to what Anthropic actually sells. The company builds Claude, the family of frontier models behind developer tools, enterprise workflows and consumer chat apps. You reach it through a coding agent like Claude Code, an enterprise integration, or a subscription on your phone.

Think of Anthropic less like a software vendor and more like a metered utility. You do not buy an annual seat licence for your team; you buy tokens, and the meter runs every time the model thinks.

That utility model makes Anthropic the first audited test case for the generative AI thesis. For three years, private rounds treated frontier labs as software companies destined for 80% gross margins. The public filing put those assumptions on a scale.

The deal was a statement. Anthropic priced at $83 a share, above a range it had already lifted, for $81.3 billion in the base offering and $93.5 billion once the greenshoe cleared.

Then it sold another $26 billion privately to the companies that supply its computing: AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Call it $119.5 billion, the biggest listing on record.

Look under the hood, and the classic software profile blurs. Footnotes imply an 85.5% gross margin for the first nine months, but only because $19.2 billion of computing cost was filed under research and development.

Total compute and infrastructure absorbed 56.6% of nine-month revenue. Intensity climbed to 58% in the third quarter, when Anthropic bought short-term capacity it says costs significantly more than contracted supply.

Meanwhile sequential growth cooled from 144% in the second quarter to 47% in the third, weighed down by $600 million of price cuts on new models.

That pressure runs into a mountain of commitments: roughly $900.9 billion of standing purchase obligations and leases, almost all of it for compute. More than $70 billion falls due over the next twelve months.

Much of that hardware comes from Amazon and Google, which are its hosts, its distribution channel and, at 14.7% and 13.7% of the capital, its largest shareholders.

The contractual backlog is just $13.8 billion, barely two months of run-rate revenue. That is what a business built on metered usage looks like: a customer can dial back whenever budgets tighten.

So the bear case is that Anthropic is not a software company at all. It is a compute wholesaler trapped in a narrowing spread. It rents processing from Google, Amazon and Broadcom, wraps it in proprietary algorithms and resells the output at a markup competition is eroding.

Pricing power is already softening, as those concessions showed. And with roughly 6% of the shares floating, a supply shock approaches: about 1.6 times the entire IPO volume unlocks by early February.

The public also owns the cash flows, not the company. A single share held by the founders' LLC carries 50.1% of voting power, and a long-term benefit trust picks a majority of the board.

The print that proves the shorts right is fourth-quarter revenue below $21 billion while compute stays at or above 58% of sales.

For the equity to re-rate, Anthropic has to show that efficiency gains reach the income statement. The market needs compute below 50% of revenue for two consecutive quarters while sales keep compounding near 25% a quarter.

The demand engine is already hot. Organizations spending at least $100,000 a year climbed to 11,900 from 950, net revenue retention sits near 900%, and Claude Code went from launch to a $2.5 billion annual run-rate inside a year.

If high-margin agents displace raw token sales, the wholesale trap disappears.

What we are watching is the fourth-quarter report, the first place investors can see whether efficiency gains outrun the server bills. The era of valuing artificial intelligence on promise ended quietly this week.

Anthropic handed the public the invoice. Now every token has to pay for itself.
